title: Saubhari and the fish
hookLine: after years of austerity under the river, a sage watches a fish with its family, and an old desire wakes
carry: desire has no beginning, but it can end
last: GOOD AND BAD BOTH BIND; OFFER THE ACT.

cards: In the Bhagavata Purana, the sage Saubhari spends years in austerity under the waters of the Yamuna, still as a stone. One day he watches a king of fish playing in the river with its mates and its little ones.
Something stirs in the sage, a wish he thought was long gone: a family, a home, a life like that. So he climbs out and goes to King Mandhata, who has fifty daughters, and asks for one.

teach.b: The king looks at this thin old ascetic and stalls: my daughters choose for themselves. So Saubhari uses his yogic power to make himself young and handsome, and all fifty choose him.
He builds them palaces and lives a life of every pleasure, and it never feels like enough. At last he sees it.

teach.h: I FELL BECAUSE OF A FISH.
teach.b: A whole life of tapas, he says, and I fell because I kept company with a fish. One sight had woken a desire that was waiting all along. He gives it up, goes back to the forest, and the story says he found freedom.
Patanjali gives the reason in two sutras. 4.10: the traces of desire, vasanas, have no beginning, because the wish to go on living is everlasting.
You can't find the first craving; there isn't one. That's the Hindu teaching of samsara: the round of births has no starting point. But 4.11 turns the key.
The traces are held up by four supports: a cause, a result, a place in the mind to rest, and an object to lean on.

Take the supports away, and the traces go. Saubhari's object was a happy fish. His own advice afterward, in the Bhagavata: if you want freedom, stay out of company lost in pleasure, and keep company with great souls.

teach.h: SATSANG: THE COMPANY OF THE GOOD.
teach.b: Hindus call that satsang, the company of the good. It's why families sing bhajans together and sit with the wise. Not because the past can be erased, but because what you feed grows.

teach.h: DESIRE HAS NO BEGINNING, BUT IT CAN END.
teach.b: So: no beginning, and still, an end.

how: Hindus speak of vasanas and samskaras carried from life to life in a samsara without beginning, and value satsang, the company of the good, in bhajan singing, temple gatherings and time with the wise; the Yoga Sutras teach removing what supports the traces rather than hunting for their origin.

o: a breath practice that burns away old desire
a deep trace of desire, laid down by past action
a craving that began in one moment of childhood

games.q: what holds the traces — tap the pairs.
p: the object that woke the trace

s: Hindus teach there was a first life where karma began
samsara is held to have no beginning; 4.10 says the traces have none.
beginningless does not mean endless here
without their four supports, the traces fall away.
Saubhari's long austerities had erased his old desire
one sight of the fish woke a trace that had been waiting.

games.q: an old habit you thought you'd beaten comes back. following Saubhari and sutra 4.11, where do you put your effort?
o: trace it back to the very first time.
change what's feeding it: the object, the company.
be ashamed; a real practitioner wouldn't have it.
games.why: the traces have no first moment, but they rest on supports. Saubhari's advice: choose your company. take away the supports, and the traces go.

practice: Let a small want come up on its own: to check the phone, to shift, to get up. Don't ask where it started; ask what it's leaning on right now, a thought, a sound, an itch, and name it quietly.
Then, if you pray, end with a few lines of a bhajan or a name of God you love: good company for the mind. If you don't, end with one line you trust.

wordCard.voice: Vasana, the trace desire leaves behind, like a scent left in cloth. These traces have no first moment, because the will to live has none, but they rest on supports, and without them they fall away.

orig.note: Sanskrit vāsanā: a lingering trace or scent, the deep impression desire leaves behind.

carryVoice: Your line: desire has no beginning, but it can end. Choose what you feed, and the company you keep. A week, done.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutra 4.11 (cause, result, substrate and object hold the traces)
Yoga Sutra 4.10, Vyasa's commentary (the wish to go on being, in every creature)
Bhagavata Purana 9.6.38–9.6.55 (Saubhari under the Yamuna, the king of fish, Mandhata's daughters, his regret and advice on company)
